content: INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS TIMES au NEWSLETTER SIGNUP My account Log Out Aug 24, 5:01 AM AEST Business News Sports Technology Entertainment NEWSLETTER My account Log Out Australia edition Business News Sports Technology Entertainment Editions Australia India International Singapore United Kingdom United States NEWSLETTER Follow Us Editions Australia India International Singapore United Kingdom United States Life Health & Wellbeing Health & Medicine COVID-19 Cases Growing in All 50 States as 'Nimbus' Variant Drives Late-Summer Surge Nationwide CDC Reports Nationwide Increase in COVID-19 Infections as Summer Ends By Jerry Thompson Published 08/21/26 AT 11:14 PM AEST Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on Pocket COVID-19 Cases Growing in All 50 States as 'Nimbus' Variant Drives Late-Summer Surge Nationwide COVID-19 infections are growing or likely growing in all 50 states, according to the latest estimates from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, marking a dramatic nationwide expansion of the virus's seasonal summer wave just as students return to school and Americans wrap up summer travel. As of Aug. 12, 2026, the CDC's Current Epidemic Trends model estimated that COVID-19 infections were growing or likely growing in 50 states and declining or likely declining in zero states, with the agency reporting no estimate available for Iowa due to insufficient data. According to the CDC's own modeling summary, that leaves the entire country, apart from Iowa's data gap, showing an upward trajectory in transmission for the first time this summer. The shift represents a striking reversal from conditions just weeks earlier. According to Newsweek, on July 22 the CDC had estimated infections were growing or likely growing in only 37 states, with 11 states showing little change in transmission at the time. By mid-August, those stable pockets had disappeared entirely from the map, with 47 states now classified as "Growing" and New Hampshire, Rhode Island and the District of Columbia categorized as "Likely Growing." In many states, the CDC estimates there is greater than a 99% probability that infections are actively increasing. The reversal is even more pronounced compared with earlier this summer. According to a report from Political.org, the CDC had estimated infections were declining or likely declining in 41 states, with growth seen in just one state, as recently as June 2. The speed of that turnaround reflects a now-familiar seasonal pattern public health officials have observed for several consecutive years. Andrew Pekosz, a professor of molecular microbiology and immunology at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, described the current surge as consistent with an established late-summer pattern. "This looks like a pattern that has been documented in the past few years," Pekosz told Newsweek, referring to the recurring late-summer and early-fall increase in COVID-19 transmission the country has experienced in recent years. Dr. John Brooks, an infectious disease physician at Emory University in Atlanta who previously worked at the CDC, offered a similar assessment while acknowledging the psychological gap between public perception and current data. "I think most of us kind of feel like it's fading away and are certainly very grateful for that," Brooks said. "But nationally we're seeing it ticking up pretty much everywhere." Wastewater surveillance data has provided further confirmation of the trend's scale. Amanda Bidwell, scientific program manager for WastewaterSCAN, told Today.com that viral concentrations detected in wastewater samples have risen sharply this month. "So far in August, SARS-CoV-2 concentrations are up 106% compared to July 2026," Bidwell said, adding that the West and South currently show the highest concentrations nationally. Despite the widespread geographic growth, health officials have emphasized that overall COVID-19 activity remains comparatively low and that the surge has not translated into a significant strain on hospitals. According to the CDC, as of Aug. 14, the amount of acute respiratory illness prompting people to seek medical care remains very low overall, even as COVID-19 activity specifically is increasing in the West and South. Emergency department visits tied to COVID-19 have similarly remained low, according to multiple outlets citing CDC data. Dr. Patrick Koo, division chief of pulmonology and critical care at Erlanger Hospital, said fewer patients are seeking emergency care for COVID-19 compared with earlier phases of the pandemic, attributing the shift both to the virus's evolution and to more people managing mild illness at home. "The virus has, of course, gone through multiple passes and mutations, and therefore the symptoms of COVID-19 are now much much milder compared to what we saw during the pandemic, so I think that if we take proper precautions and you know try to practice good hand hygiene to stay away from others that are sick for until they get better, of course, and that would minimize a lot of the transmission," Koo said. He added that current seasonal patterns should not cause alarm. "We do see periodic rises in certain months usually in the summer and then also in the winter as well so and so I think that there's no there's nothing to be alarmed about COVID-19 right now," Koo said. The current wave has been driven primarily by a variant known as NB.1.8.1, commonly referred to as "Nimbus," a descendant of the JN.1 Omicron lineage that had already accounted for an estimated 43% of circulating cases by late June, according to Political.org's reporting. Separately, a more heavily mutated strain known as BA.3.2, nicknamed "Cicada," has been spreading globally since emerging earlier this year, though it has not gained significant traction within the United States. According to Today.com, roughly 15% of current U.S. cases are attributed to the Cicada variant, even as no major new mutation has driven the current wave beyond the continued spread of Nimbus. Public health researchers have noted that COVID-19's biannual surge pattern, occurring in both summer and winter, remains distinct from more familiar seasonal illnesses such as influenza, which typically peaks only during colder months. The precise biological reason behind COVID-19's dual seasonality remains unclear, according to reporting from Political.org, though experts have pointed to a combination of factors, including waning immunity following winter infections, increased indoor gatherings in air-conditioned spaces during hot summer months, and continued summer travel patterns, as likely contributors to the recurring late-July and August peaks the country has now experienced for three consecutive years. Symptoms associated with the current wave remain broadly consistent with those seen in earlier omicron-lineage variants, typically appearing within two to 14 days of exposure. According to the CDC, common symptoms continue to include fever, cough, fatigue, congestion, sore throat, and loss of taste or smell, among other cold- and flu-like signs. As students return to classrooms and colder weather approaches in the coming months, health officials are likely to continue monitoring whether the current nationwide growth trend persists, plateaus or begins to recede, following the pattern of prior late-summer surges. This story includes information on a virus that can pose greater risk to certain populations. If you are concerned about COVID-19 symptoms or exposure, particularly if you are immunocompromised, elderly or otherwise at higher risk, consult a health care provider for personalized guidance. Written byStephanie Edwards Stephanie Edwards Stephanie Edwards is the Engagement Specialist at Discover Magazine, who manages all social media platforms and writes digital articles that focus on archaeology, the environment, and public health. Aug 20, 2026, 8:49 PM | 3 min read (Image Credit: PeopleImages/Shutterstock) Newsletter Sign up for our email newsletter for the latest science news Sign Up Long before a needle touches the skin, your immune system may have already decided how it's going to respond. Hidden among the antibodies circulating in a person’s blood could be signs of whether an upcoming vaccine will trigger a powerful defense or a comparatively weak response. Vaccines protect most people from severe disease, but their effectiveness is not identical in everyone. A new study published in Cell Press Blue suggests researchers may be able to anticipate some of that variation using pre-vaccination blood samples and artificial intelligence. The findings could eventually help doctors identify people who may benefit from extra doses, closer monitoring, or other protective measures. “What our study found is that certain biomarkers, when analyzed with AI, can predict who is likely to respond well to a vaccine, even before they receive it. This suggests that some people may be more immune-ready than others,” said study lead Joshua LaBaer in a press release. Preexisting Antibodies May Predict Vaccine Response Researchers examined blood samples from more than 4,000 people, measuring antibodies that reacted to 185 antigens. These immune targets included components of familiar viruses and bacteria, along with markers connected to autoimmune diseases. The team compared antibody patterns recorded before and after COVID-19 vaccination. They discovered that elevated levels of several preexisting antibodies were associated with stronger responses to the vaccine, including common microbes like Staphylococcus aureus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and human respirovirus 3. The scientists suggest these are “sentinel” antibodies because they are not necessarily helping the body attack the vaccine’s intended target. Instead, they may serve as signals of how prepared the antibody-producing portion of the immune system is to spring into action. Read More: COVID-19 Is Spreading Again as a Summer Wave Grows Across the U.S. Why Vaccine Protection Varies Between People Scientists typically assess vaccine response after a vaccine, measuring the antibodies generated against a particular target. This study reversed the question by asking whether someone’s existing immune landscape could forecast their reaction before vaccination. Age, biological sex, genetics, previous infections, and underlying medical conditions can all influence vaccine responses. Immunosuppressive medications or illnesses can also limit the immune system’s ability to react. Yet broad health categories do not tell the entire story. Several immunosuppressed groups in the study were most likely to produce weaker responses, but some immunosuppressed participants still responded strongly. Meanwhile, approximately 5 to 6 percent of otherwise healthy participants had weak responses. That inconsistency suggests immune readiness cannot always be determined from a person’s diagnosis or general health status alone. How AI Could Help Personalize Future Vaccines Rather than relying on one antibody, the researchers trained a deep-learning model to examine patterns across the entire panel. By combining numerous measurements into a larger immune fingerprint, the system could distinguish stronger vaccine responders from weaker ones. This is where AI offers a particular advantage. Biological datasets can contain millions of overlapping data points, making meaningful connections difficult for humans to spot. Machine-learning models can search that complexity for subtle combinations that carry predictive value. The results suggest researchers may learn more by viewing immunity as a landscape shaped by many past encounters with microbes, rather than checking for antibodies against only one pathogen. Although the study focused on COVID-19 vaccination, the method could have wider applications. With further validation, sentinel antibody profiles might support vaccine development and help clinicians recognize patients who need additional doses, follow-up testing, or alternative protection. The future of vaccination may therefore involve more than choosing the right shot — it may also mean understanding the immune system receiving it. Assam Fresh Covid-19 cases rise in Assam since June; experts rule out severe threat Patients infected with the RF.5 Covid-19 variant are largely showing flu-like symptoms, with no evidence so far of severe illness By Staff Correspondent - 22 Aug 2026 5:54 AM X Representational image (Photo: PTI) The Assam Tribune is now on Whatsapp. Click here to join our channel and stay updated with the latest headlines. Guwahati, Aug 22: Fresh cases of Covid-19 have been reported in Assam over the past two months, but health experts say the infections detected so far have not been severe. Officials said that around 80-90 positive cases were reported in upper Assam during July and August. Also Read - Assam-Meghalaya row: Different resolution timelines emerge after Aug-23 talks The Covid-19 variant circulating in India since June 2026 belongs to the RF.5 subvariant of Omicron, which emerged from the JN.1 lineage. “Patients are showing flu-like or influenza-like symptoms. There is no evidence so far to suggest that RF.5 is causing severe infections,” a microbiologist said. Also Read - Tezpur University VC row: 7 months on, Centre yet to decide on inquiry report Covid-19 cases were also reported in Assam in 2025, with the last cases recorded in December. “However, the latest increase in cases has been observed since the end of June 2026. Also Read - Nagaland group challenges Assam eviction drive in Golaghat, claims disputed land Officials said that Covid-19 has now become a recurring viral illness, with new variants likely to cause periodic waves of infection. During the recent resurgence of Covid-19 in Andhra Pradesh, health authorities observed that those who succumbed to the infection had underlying chronic conditions, including diabetes and hypertension. Senior citizens, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions such as diabetes, hypertension and kidney disease continue to remain at greater risk of complications. content: 24/7 LiveRaleighDurhamFayettevilleSurrounding Area 87° COVID 19 COVID-19 activity rising as students head back to school, experts say ByBianca Holman Wednesday, August 19, 2026 4:53PM As summer ends, COVID-19 activity is increasing across the United States, according to health officials. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimate that COVID-19 transmission is rising nationwide. While overall activity levels remain low, infectious disease experts say the virus is spreading more quickly in some regions, particularly in the South. Doctors say seasonal patterns and human behavior often contribute to increases in COVID-19 cases. One spike typically occurs as families return from summer travel and students head back to school. Another increase is commonly seen during the winter months when people spend more time indoors. COVID-19 spreads primarily from person to person through respiratory droplets and aerosols. Common symptoms include cough, sore throat, congestion, fatigue, fever, chills and headaches. Health experts also continue to monitor long COVID, a condition involving lingering symptoms that can persist for weeks or months after an initial infection. Dr. David Wohl, an infectious disease specialist with UNC Health, said new treatment options are available for people who have been exposed to the virus but have not yet developed symptoms. "Let's say someone in your household, your child or somebody else gets COVID-19," Wohl said. "There's now a medicine that was approved at the end of May that you can take that can help prevent infection after exposure. You've been exposed, you're not sick yet, but you're worried and you don't want to get sick." He added that Paxlovid remains available for people who develop COVID-19 and qualify for treatment. Doctors recommend that people who become sick with COVID-19 stay home and limit contact with others until their symptoms improve. An updated COVID-19 vaccine is not yet available, but health care providers expect new doses to arrive in September. Public health officials continue to encourage people to stay informed about local transmission levels, monitor symptoms and seek medical guidance if they believe they have been exposed to the virus. Abstract Social correction has been shown to be effective in reducing misperceptions and limiting the production of harmful content online, but most current evidence comes from platform-run systems or controlled experiments. We evaluate a volunteer-led intervention on Facebook in which trained healthcare workers replied to COVID-19 vaccine-related posts and comments. The intervention used two sources of random variation: randomized ordering of posts on volunteers’ worklists and random assignment of whether drafted replies were posted. We estimate effects on post-level engagement metrics, distinguishing diffusion indicators, measured by shares; interaction indicators, measured by comments; and affective indicators, measured by likes and reactions. The intervention reduced comments on treated posts, with broader declines in some affective responses in randomized-treatment analyses, especially for newer posts and posts classified as anti-vaccine. We find little evidence of reduced sharing. Our results indicate changes in some forms of engagement with treated posts; they do not directly demonstrate reductions in misinformation prevalence, belief change, or exposure patterns. Appendices Appendix A: additional intervention details Ethics This project was approved by the University of Calgary Joint Ethics Board (REB22-0315_REN1). The intervention described in the paper was performed in accordance with the guidelines and regulations required by this board. Volunteer recruitment and training Our goal at the beginning of the project was to recruit up to 50 volunteers who were either health care professionals (doctors, nurses, pharmacists, or public health workers) or students in health-related fields. We attempt to recruit using a variety of methods, including (i) advertising on the website of 19 to Zero, our partner organization, (ii) posting on 19 to Zero’s social media accounts, (iii) sending emails to 19 to Zero’s existing volunteer and contact base, and (iv) reaching out to health-related university programs in Canada and asking them to send materials to their students. The advertising material we used offered potential volunteers a chance to combat vaccine hesitancy online and to earn a $300 honorarium and Health Leadership Certificate. Interested individuals were invited to attend online information sessions that were held in mid-2022. Approximately 60 potential volunteers attended the initial information sessions on Zoom, which provided an overview of the goals of the projects and the work that we expected volunteers to do, and provided an opportunity for interested individuals to ask questions to the research team. Following the information session, all participants were contacted by email outlining next steps for a potential engagement. Individuals who indicated an interest in volunteering with us were invited to a further 30 min training session. Prior to attending the session, they were asked to read training materials outlining (i) behavioral principles for combatting vaccine hesitancy, including “good” and “bad” responses to real comments from social media, (ii) tips for how to identify productive conversation opportunities – and which individuals to avoid, and (iii) instructions for how to engage online in a safe way. The training materials are available upon request. During training sessions, volunteers were provided with links to Facebook posts and asked to identify which, if any, comments they would engage with and explain why. They were given feedback on their choices by the research team and other participants. They were then asked to formulate a potential response to comments, and again given feedback. This process was repeated 2–3 times, depending on time constraints. Following training, volunteers were provided with summary documents outlining the process for engagement and the main behavioral principles they should adhere to, as well as links to helpful information on the vaccines. They were also given access to the list of Facebook posts meeting our search criteria. In total, 14 volunteers completed training and went on to participate in the project. Most of these volunteers completed the 30 h we requested in order to be eligible for the honorarium and certificate. Several volunteers signed up for an additional 30 h commitment after this point, and were given an additional honorarium at the end of this commitment. Our volunteers were mostly students, but also included a small number of working health professionals. Process Prior to beginning work with us, volunteers were encouraged to create new Facebook accounts that were not linked to their real Facebook accounts, and that used a version of their names that could not be used to identify them (i.e. “John S.”) and a picture that did not show their faces. They were also encouraged to be honest about the purpose for these accounts by posting information in the biography section indicating that they were health professionals or students, and that they used these accounts to have conversations about the COVID-19 vaccine. When leaving a comment, volunteers were permitted (but not required) to tell people that they were working on behalf of a public health organization. We asked volunteers to friend the Informed Choice Project’s Facebook account with their secondary accounts so that we could keep track of their activity. Volunteers were permitted to work whenever they wanted, although we asked them to put in a minimum of 2 h per week. The process volunteers were asked to follow when completing volunteer hours was: 1) Open key documents, which included: the summary instruction materials we had provided, the sheet with links to vaccine information, and the list of Facebook posts identified by our search. 2) Starting at the top of the list of Facebook posts, open any post that had not yet been worked on by another volunteer (indicated by volunteers putting their names next to the post in the sheet) and read the post and the comments on it. The goal was to identify whether there were any productive engagement opportunities. 3) Once the volunteer decided to leave a comment, they were instructed to open a survey tool in Qualtrics and enter the following information: their name, the link to the post, the name of the individual leaving an original comment (when leaving a reply), and the text of the original comment (when leaving a reply). The tool then randomly instructed them to either leave the comment or not. 4) If they were instructed to leave a comment, they were asked to craft a reply that followed behavioral principles and was based on real information about the vaccine. The information they used to craft this comment could come from our information sources, or they could try to find other information from reputable sources as required. They were then asked to enter the text of their reply into the survey tool, as well as posting it on Facebook. 5) Repeat until they were done a given work session. Once they finished working, they were asked to log their hours using an online volunteer engagement system. The hours were verified by the research team using the information in the Qualtrics database (i.e. we ensured that the volunteer was active in leaving replies during the indicated hours). Data gathering Following the end of the intervention, we downloaded the Qualtrics data containing information about every attempted reply by our volunteers. There were 1,683 attempted replies, of which 174 could not be linked to a URL appearing on our list because of incorrect entry into the “link” field of our form, and 4 appeared to have incorrect dates. The remaining 1,505 attempts were distributed over 736 posts. We used CrowdTangle to get engagement information on every post that ever appeared on our list. We gathered the full engagement history for each of these posts, and then restricted the set of engagement observations to three per post (earliest at least 2 days after creation, latest pre-treatment, latest). We randomly selected a subset of 1,470 non-targeted posts to serve as a control group. Of the 2,206 combined posts, 214 did not have any engagement information available from CrowdTangle (this could occur, for example, if the post was taken down between the time we searched for it and the time when we gathered engagement information). A further 26 were not available as of January 2024, when the research team began the sentiment rating process. A further 34 posts were eliminated because the engagement information provided did not cover both the pre and post treatment period. Finally, 21 posts were eliminated because they were strong outliers on pre-post engagement changes. These restrictions led to a final sample of 2,118 posts, of which 709 had any attempted treatment (273 never treated, 436 treated), and 1,409 did not. Appendix figure 11 below shows the creation of the sample visually, including the number of posts of each type that were lost due to each of the sample restrictions. Measuring vaccine sentiment of posts and comments For parts of the analysis that classify either posts or comments as “pro-vaccine”, “neutral”, or “anti-vaccine”, we relied on researcher ratings of vaccine sentiment. The research team worked from a list of posts presented in random order without any information about treatment. They opened the post and read it, and rated it on a scale from − 10 (very anti-vaccine) to 10 (very pro-vaccine). They then did the same for the first two pre-intervention comments on a post. Two raters attempted to rate each post. Because Meta restricted news to Canadian audiences starting in July 2023, raters could not access all posts from Canada at the time rating started in January 2024. One rater was sent to the United States to complete rating for these posts. Anti-vaccine posts and comments could be either directly related to the vaccine, or related to other types of misinformation relevant to the vaccine (in particular, the effectiveness of masking and the use of ivermectin as a treatment for COVID-19). News headlines, particularly from mainstream news organizations, were typically rated as neutral. Pro-vaccine posts were most commonly announcements from public health organizations encouraging the use of the vaccine–although there were also posts from fact-checking and pro-science organizations included in this group. When rating posts and comments, the researchers took into account sentiment on issues that were highly correlated with attitudes about the vaccine, including: the efficacy of masking, the belief that the COVID-19 pandemic was a government conspiracy, the efficacy of Ivermectin as a treatment for COVID, the belief that COVID-19 was “just a cold”, etc. Posts or comments supporting these positions were rated as anti-vaccine. News stories from major outlets about the vaccine were typically rated as neutral, unless they were written in a way that was clearly pro- or anti-vaccine. Appendix B: Robustness checks Excluding non-compliant volunteers As noted in the main paper, there were two volunteers for whom we could not verify any of the comments they recorded. We are unclear as to whether these volunteers left the comments and deleted them at the end of the intervention, or never left the comments. Appendix figure 12 shows how the results for the main sample change if we exclude posts treated by these volunteers. The results are nearly identical, but slightly stronger if we exclude these posts. Outlier management In the course of analysis, we noticed that there were some strong outliers that saw very strong changes in engagement from the pre-intervention to post-intervention period. Appendix figure 13 shows the raw change in the engagement index from pre- to post-intervention, plotted against randomized rank order. As the figure shows, these observations are mostly untreated and most (but not all) appeared towards the bottom of the volunteers’ list. The latter feature means that they have the potential to create a relationship between engagement and rank or treatment that is not driven by the intervention. In our main results, we eliminate these observations by excluding 21 posts that have changes in the engagement index (residualized after accounting for control variables) that are more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean. Appendix figure 14 shows how the results change when we do not impose this restriction. When outliers are included, the results for randomized rank order become 10–20 times larger and are statistically significant for 4 of the 6 outcomes. The randomized treatment results remain relatively similar to those in the main text, although are slightly smaller and less statistically significant. The size of the rank order results when including outliers suggests that the relationships they document between rank order and engagement are not purely due to rank order affecting treatment. For example, the implied IV effect of treatment on the engagement index in this case is 0.069 SD – about 15 times higher than the effect we estimate using random treatment. Because this result is driven by a small number of observations, we consider it more prudent to exclude these observations. Note that while the relative magnitude of the results is sensitive to the inclusion of outliers, the main conclusion of the paper – that our intervention reduced some forms of engagement – holds in both cases. We unpacked the federal grant and research fueling the conspiracy theory. Megan Loe August 23, 2026 SUNDAY READ Welcome to this special edition of Snopes’ newsletter. Today, we’re investigating a persistent rumor claiming Dr. Fauci funded research that allegedly caused the COVID-19 pandemic. Did Fauci fund Chinese research that caused COVID-19? More than six years after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, gaps in our knowledge about its origin are still fueling speculation and conspiracy theories. One persistent rumor accuses Dr. Anthony Fauci of funding research at a lab in China that supposedly created a genetically modified virus and caused the pandemic. While the allegations are based on real, NIH-funded research into bat coronaviruses, the narrative draws conclusions that aren’t backed by evidence. In this exclusive report, we unpack: The competing theories behind the pandemic’s origin. The debate over “gain-of-function” research. The federal grant fueling the conspiracy theory involving Fauci. By Marcela Camargo • Published August 22, 2026 • Updated on August 22, 2026 at 3:01 pm Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER Live Unmute Subtitles EnglishNoneSettings ShareToggle Fullscreen Look who it is. A New Jersey real estate investor pleaded guilty earlier this week to participating in a multimillion-dollar mortgage fraud scheme and fraudulently obtaining more than $1.8 million in COVID-19 relief loans, according to U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer. Officials said 39-year-old Arthur Spitzer, of Toms River, pleaded guilty Wednesday to one count of bank and wire fraud conspiracy and one count of money laundering in connection with the fraud schemes. Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10. WATCH HERE According to prosecutors, who cited court documents and statements made in court, in June 2020, Spitzer conspired with Mendel Deutsch and Joshua Feldberger, who are both awaiting sentencing, to make it appear as though Spitzer owned three properties in Brooklyn, New York, and had agreed to sell them to Deutsch, who obtained a $4.5 million mortgage loan in connection with the transaction. Prosecutors said Feldberger facilitated the fraudulent transaction as the owner of the settlement company that handled it. According to officials, the defendants also created and sent letters stating that Deutsch had deposited significant funds into escrow toward the transaction when, in reality, he had not. Instead, they created fake documentation purportedly transferring control of the properties to Spitzer and made false statements to the mortgage lender, claiming that the settlement company had received more than $2 million from Deutsch at closing. Those statements led the mortgage lender to fund the loan. The men then used the mortgage loan proceeds to fund Deutsch’s down payment, which he had supposedly already provided, prosecutors said. According to officials, Spitzer also admitted that he was responsible for the losses resulting from five additional fraudulent loan schemes in 2019 and 2020, totaling more than $10 million. The CARES Act authorized the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) to provide Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDLs) of up to $2 million to eligible small businesses that were experiencing substantial financial disruption due to the COVID-19 pandemic. To obtain an EIDL loan, a qualifying small business was required to submit an application and provide information on its operations, including the number of employees and revenues or expenses. Prosecutors said Spitzer obtained EIDLs for businesses with little or no operations by submitting loan applications containing false statements about the applicant companies’ number of employees, revenues, cost of goods sold or lost rents. According to officials, Spitzer then laundered some of the proceeds from the EIDL fraud. The bank and wire fraud conspiracy count is punishable by a maximum of 30 years in prison and a $1 million fine, or twice the gross gain or loss from the offense. The money laundering count is punishable by a maximum of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, or twice the gross gain or loss from the offense. Spitzer has agreed to pay full restitution to the victims, including $1 million to the true owner of the Brooklyn properties and at least $1,845,400 to the SBA, subject to any applicable credits for amounts already repaid to the victims. Spitzer also agreed to forfeit $2.25 million in connection with the bank and wire fraud conspiracy and $100,000 in connection with the laundering of fraudulent EIDL proceeds, for a total of $2.35 million. Spitzer is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. 21, 2026. Deutsch is scheduled to be sentenced on Oct. 6, 2026, and Feldberger is awaiting a new sentencing date. Sisti, CCRP Current Page Resha B. Sisti, CCRP Resha Sisti, CCRP, joined St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital in 2012 and currently is a Clinical Research Associate II in the Department of Bone Marrow Transplantation and Cellular Therapy. When Sisti initially arrived at St. Jude, she joined the Department of Immunology, spending 10 years engaged in immunology-focused research. Her work included projects on T cell responses, TCR diversity, and host responses to infection. During her time in the lab, she gained hands-on experience in virus recovery, generating ferret monoclonal antibodies, flow cytometry, CRISPR Cas9 gene editing, embryonic stem cell targeting and culture etc. Over time, Sisti’s interests began to shift toward clinical research. As her involvement in human studies expanded, she took oversight of multiple human sample projects within the lab, which ultimately led her to formally transition into a clinical research associate role. As the first CRA in the department, Sisti managed regulatory responsibilities for multiple human studies involving samples from collaborating sites. Working under rapidly evolving conditions during Covid19, she collaborated with multiple teams to help develop protocol, consents, establish SOPs for sample processing and distribution, and manage extensive blood sample processing efforts for SJTRC study involving SJ employees. As her experience in clinical research grew, the Kathmandu, Nepal, native sought greater exposure to patient-centered research and joined the Bone Marrow Transplantation and Cellular Therapy team. Working alongside a highly dedicated clinical research team, she has taken the lead on multiple protocols and gained experience in developing studies from the ground up. In BMTCT, she is a part of the hematologic malignancy team and has been involved with the Transplant, Virus Specific T cell and CAR-T protocols. Collaborating across departments has reinforced her understanding that successful clinical research is a collective effort, with each team contributing unique expertise toward improving patient outcomes. Pursuing a master's degree in the St. Jude Graduate Schools’ Clinical Investigations program represents an opportunity to deepen her understanding of clinical research from a broader and more structured perspective. Sisti aims to apply the skills gained through this program to advance her career, take on mentorship and leadership roles, and contribute to the development and execution of impactful clinical protocols. Sisti believes the program will provide the knowledge, skills, and confidence necessary to help her achieve these goals and continue growing as a clinical research professional.
